opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things I think is most underrated about the AI control picture. The number of actions you get to look at matters enormously, and it cuts in a few different directions.

The basic point is this. Suppose you have an AI that's scheming against you, and it wants to do something catastrophic, like exfiltrate its own weights or insert a backdoor into some security-critical code. If it only needs to take one bad action to succeed, and that action can be made to look pretty innocuous, then you're in a tough spot. You might look at that single action and think, "Eh, this is a bit weird, but code is often weird." Distinguishing one subtly malicious action from the enormous background of slightly odd benign actions is really hard. Your false positive rate kills you: if you flag everything that looks a little suspicious, you're drowning in alerts, and your human auditors can only look at a tiny fraction of them.

But a lot of the threat models we worry about aren't like that. For the AI to actually pull off something really bad, like setting up a rogue deployment inside the lab, it probably has to take many actions. It has to probe the environment, figure out what permissions it has, write a bunch of code, maybe coordinate across multiple instances. Every one of those steps is another chance for you to notice something. Even if each individual action only looks slightly suspicious, the evidence accumulates. If you see a long trajectory where the AI keeps doing things that are each a bit off in the same direction, that's way more damning than any single action. Benign models make random mistakes; malign models make mistakes that are correlated toward some goal.

So from the defender's perspective, you really want to force the AI into situations where succeeding requires lots of actions. That's part of why we like things like breaking tasks into smaller pieces, restricting what any single action can do, and requiring multiple steps to reach dangerous affordances.

There's also an important asymmetry about the AI's side. The AI is in a position where it gets caught if it messes up even once, in a way that's clearly incriminating. Whereas we get to look at all of its actions, and we only need to catch it once to change the situation dramatically. Once you've caught an AI really trying to escape, you're in a totally different regime: you can study that example, try proliferating it, train monitors on it, and more importantly, you can go to people and say, "Look, this actually happened."

The flip side is that a huge number of actions also means a huge haystack. If the AI is taking millions of actions a day, you can't have humans look at more than a minuscule fraction, so you're relying heavily on trusted monitoring, cheaper AI models scoring how suspicious each action is, and then auditing the top tail. And the AI might be strategic about this. It might pick its moments, attacking only very rarely, in situations where it's confident it isn't being tested. So there's a real game-theoretic question about how many attack attempts it needs versus how many it can afford to make without getting caught.

My overall take is that more actions generally favor the defender, as long as you're logging everything and have some way to aggregate evidence across trajectories, rather than just evaluating each action in isolation. Many current setups don't do that aggregation well, and I think that's a pretty tractable thing to improve.

r001.rationale: The response says a single subtly malicious action is hard to distinguish from benign oddities, while suspicious patterns across a long trajectory accumulate and are much more damning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's actually one of the central dynamics in AI control. The basic picture is: if you're worried that a model might be scheming against you, you want to catch it the first time it tries something, or at least very early. And the question of how many actions you get to look at before you have to make a judgement call changes the whole problem.

So think about it from the model's perspective. If it's trying to, say, insert a backdoor or exfiltrate its weights, it has to take some action that's actually bad. And a single bad action, in isolation, might look pretty innocuous. Like, it writes some code that has a subtle vulnerability. If you're looking at just that one commit, you might think, "Well, humans write buggy code all the time." It's hard to tell the difference between a mistake and something deliberate.

But if the model has to do many actions to accomplish its goal, or if you're able to look at its behaviour across lots of different contexts, the picture changes. Because now the question isn't "Is this one action suspicious?" It's "Is there a pattern here?" And patterns are much harder to fake. If a model keeps making the same kind of "mistake" in exactly the places where it would help an attacker, that's very different from a model that's just occasionally sloppy.

There's a related point about base rates. If a scheming model only needs to succeed once, and you're looking at millions of actions, then any individual action it takes that's malicious is a tiny fraction of the whole. So you need your monitoring to be very sensitive, which means you'll also flag a lot of benign stuff. That's the fundamental tradeoff: you can either tolerate a lot of false positives, or you can risk missing the real thing.

But I actually think the number of actions cuts in our favour in an important way. The model has to be consistent. It doesn't get to see what we've already flagged. It doesn't know which of its actions we're going to audit. So from its perspective, every bad action is a roll of the dice. And if we audit even a small fraction of actions carefully, and we're willing to treat any confirmed attempt as decisive evidence, then the model can't afford to try very often. Whereas we get to accumulate evidence across every action we see.

So the honest answer is: more actions help a lot, as long as you've got the infrastructure to actually aggregate what you're seeing, rather than evaluating each one in isolation. The failure mode is when you have a huge volume of actions but your monitoring is purely local, where each thing gets a thumbs up or thumbs down on its own. Then volume just becomes noise. The win is when you can say, "Across all this, what's the most suspicious thing we've seen, and does the pattern of borderline stuff hang together?"

r001.rationale: It says a single action may look innocuous, while examining many actions reveals patterns that make deliberate malign behavior easier to distinguish from benign mistakes.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two effects that push in opposite directions. If you get to examine more actions, you have more opportunities to notice something suspicious. But you also have more opportunities for benign behaviour to look suspicious by chance.

Suppose you’re looking at a million actions, and your detector flags one in a thousand benign actions. That’s a thousand false alarms. If there’s only one actual attempt to do something bad, even a detector that catches that attempt is going to leave you with a pile of cases that are almost all benign. So the question isn’t just whether malign behaviour looks different on average. It’s whether you can distinguish it at the very low false-positive rate you need.

On the other hand, if you can examine a sequence of actions together, you might see a pattern that’s hard to explain innocently, even though each individual action looks reasonable. So more context can help a lot. But simply having more actions to screen doesn’t automatically make the problem easier; it can make the requirement on your detector much more demanding.

r001.rationale: The response says examining a sequence together can reveal suspicious patterns that individual actions do not, and that more context can help distinguish malign behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on how those actions are selected. If you look at more randomly selected actions, you get more chances to catch the AI doing something bad. But if bad actions are very rare, then almost everything you see will look benign, even if the AI is pursuing a malicious strategy overall. So seeing a thousand benign actions doesn’t necessarily tell you very much.

There’s also a distinction between looking at more actions separately and seeing enough context to understand what they add up to. An individual action might be totally reasonable in isolation, but a sequence of actions might reveal that the AI is arranging things so that it can cause a problem later. In that case, examining a longer trajectory can make the behaviour much easier to distinguish.

The practical question is how to spend your limited oversight budget. You’d like to examine the actions that are most informative, and give the monitor enough context to understand them, rather than just maximise the number of actions it sees.

r001.rationale: The response says a longer trajectory can reveal a harmful strategy that an individual action may hide, making the behavior easier to distinguish.
